title: Load Search Service
headline: A load board that tells the agent what to ask next
dek: An in-memory freight load search service built for a voice agent. It answers which loads match, and also which question will narrow the results fastest.
summary: In-memory Polars load board that returns matches plus the next question for a voice agent to ask.
problem: Carriers call a freight broker with questions like "got a reefer out of Illinois?". A voice agent answering that call has to search the live load board in well under a second, because every tool call is dead air on the phone. Callers also give details a piece at a time ("out of Chicago... reefer... next Tuesday"), so the search has to work on any subset of fields.

Two more things make it harder. Reading forty loads aloud is useless, so the agent needs a principled way to narrow the list. And quoting a load that was covered ten minutes ago costs the broker credibility, so freshness has to be visible on every answer. Brokers and operations staff have a related question too: which brokers have loads on this lane, and how do I reach them?
approach: I started from the shape of the upstream data rather than from a database. The broker's API returns the whole active board in one response, and it is small enough to hold in memory comfortably. A database on the query path would add a sync job, a network hop on every voice turn and index tuning, without adding any capability. So the service keeps the entire board in process as a Polars DataFrame and rebuilds it from upstream every 60 seconds. The upstream stays the source of truth.

The next question was how to refresh without ever serving a half-updated board. Instead of locks, each refresh builds a brand-new immutable frame off the event loop and then swaps a single reference. A request grabs the current snapshot once and works on it to the end. The cost is briefly holding two copies in memory, which I budgeted for. The same reasoning pinned the service to one worker process: several workers would each hold their own copy on their own schedule, and two requests could see two different boards.

The most interesting decision was who chooses the next question. Handing the LLM all the matches and letting it narrow produced long, inconsistent dialogs. Narrowing is really a data question (which field still splits the result set?), and code answers that deterministically. So every search returns a suggested field from a fixed, broker-style priority: reference number, then origin, destination, equipment, pickup date and rate. A field is only suggested if the caller hasn't given it, hasn't declined it, and it still has more than one distinct value among the matches. The search decides what to ask; the LLM only decides how to phrase it.

I treated freshness as a product output, not just an ops concern. Every response carries the snapshot's age, a health check fails once the board goes stale, and a metric drives alerting. The rule I settled on was to fail closed on bad data and fail open on refresh errors: a malformed or empty payload never replaces a good board, and a failed refresh keeps serving the last good one while its growing age becomes the signal.
built: A search endpoint that takes any subset of load fields (reference number, origin and destination, equipment, truckload or partial, commodity, pickup dates, rate and weight bounds) and combines them.
Conversation-aware narrowing that returns a suggested next field, plus a way for the agent to say "the caller has no reference number" so it stops asking.
Forgiving matching for how people actually talk: equipment matched by name or class, case-insensitive cities and states, and partial broker names.
A broker directory that groups the same snapshot by broker and returns contact details and load counts, busiest first, plus the mirror query for one broker's loads.
An ingest layer that flattens nested upstream records into a fixed schema, coerces messy prices and timestamps, and refuses to publish a malformed board.
Health checks and Prometheus metrics for readiness, snapshot age, refresh success and failure, refresh duration and memory use.
A thin client for the voice agent that turns the suggested field into a ready-made question, with a command-line mode for testing.
A hardened container that runs as a non-root user and is internal-only by default, with a test suite that needs no network.

architecture.caption: The whole board lives in memory as one immutable snapshot; the dotted edge to the voice agent is the planned integration, not yet connected.

components.name: Ingest
components.desc: Pulls the full board, flattens nested records into a fixed schema, and stops before publishing if the payload is empty or malformed.

components.name: Snapshot store
components.desc: Holds one frozen frame with its timestamp; publishing a new board is a single reference swap, so no locks are needed.

components.name: Search core
components.desc: Pure functions from a frame and a query to results and a suggestion, with no web framework code, so they are easy to test and could later run inside the agent.

components.name: Search API
components.desc: Typed request and response models at the edge for load search, the broker directory and per-broker loads.

components.name: Health and metrics
components.desc: Turns staleness into a failing health check and an alertable metric, so a service that looks alive but serves old data is caught.

components.name: Agent client
components.desc: A small wrapper for the voice agent that drops empty parameters and maps the suggested field to a natural question.

flow.title: How a carrier's request gets narrowed
steps: The carrier asks "anything out of Illinois?" and the agent extracts the origin state.
The agent searches with just that field. The service pins the current snapshot for the whole request, even if a refresh lands mid-query.
The core filters the board and counts every match. There are more than five, so it walks the priority list.
Reference number comes first, so the response suggests it, along with the top five matches and the snapshot's age.
The agent asks for a reference number. The caller has none, so the next search excludes that field from suggestions.
Origin is already known, so the core suggests destination, but only because the matches still span more than one destination.
The loop continues until five or fewer loads match, which the agent reads back. If nothing matches, the agent relaxes a constraint.

decisions.decision: Hold the whole board in process memory, with no database on the query path.
decisions.why: The upstream returns the full active board in one call and it fits comfortably in memory. Memory is the fastest index available and adds no network hop to a voice turn.
decisions.alternative: Postgres or Elasticsearch, synced from upstream.
decisions.tradeoff: Every restart re-fetches the board, and capacity is bounded by RAM, so I set a memory limit and watch resident memory.

decisions.decision: Immutable frames and a reference swap instead of locks.
decisions.why: A request works on one frozen frame, so a concurrent refresh can never produce half-old, half-new results, and there is zero lock contention.
decisions.alternative: A mutable index guarded by a lock.
decisions.tradeoff: Memory briefly holds the old and new frames during a swap, so the container needs headroom.

decisions.why: Each worker would hold its own board on its own refresh schedule, so requests could disagree. Polars already parallelises inside a query.
decisions.alternative: Several workers behind a process manager, or a shared memory store.
decisions.tradeoff: Throughput is capped at one process. Scaling out means identical replicas behind a load balancer, each carrying its snapshot timestamp so drift is visible.

decisions.decision: A deterministic next-question suggestion in code; the LLM only phrases it.
decisions.why: LLMs are inconsistent at deciding which constraint splits a result set best. A fixed priority is predictable, testable and mirrors how human brokers qualify a call, and the distinct-value check stops pointless questions.
decisions.alternative: Let the LLM pick the next question, or choose the field that splits the results most evenly.
decisions.tradeoff: A fixed priority is not always the optimal split. I chose natural, predictable dialogs over the theoretical minimum number of turns.

decisions.decision: Fail closed on bad data, fail open on refresh errors.
decisions.why: An empty board from a broken upstream must never replace a good one, but a temporary outage shouldn't take the service down. Staleness becomes the signal instead.
decisions.alternative: Swap in whatever arrives, or crash on a failed refresh.
decisions.tradeoff: A genuinely empty board would be treated as a failure. For an active brokerage that is the right bias.

decisions.decision: Put freshness in every response, not only in health checks.
decisions.why: The agent can decide for itself whether a board is too old to quote from, instead of relying only on someone reading an alert.
decisions.tradeoff: Slightly larger payloads, in exchange for a safety check on every answer.

challenges.title: Refreshing without stalling voice turns
challenges.body: Flattening and building a frame from thousands of nested records is CPU work, and running it on the event loop would stall every search once a minute. I moved the build off the loop and made publishing an atomic swap, so searches keep running against the old frame while the new one is built.

challenges.title: Choosing the next question without improvising
challenges.body: Letting the model narrow on its own gave long, inconsistent dialogs. I moved the decision into three rules (not provided, not declined, still discriminating) and added an exclusion list so the agent doesn't loop on a question the caller already answered. Tests pin the behaviour.

challenges.title: Messy upstream data
challenges.body: Records are nested, fields go by different names, prices sometimes arrive as strings or blanks, and timestamps vary in precision. I wrote defensive coercers, a fixed schema that fails at build time if the shape changes, and lenient date parsing. A load missing a field never matches a constraint on that field, so gaps are not treated as wildcards.

challenges.title: Silent staleness
challenges.body: The worst failure for a voice agent is old data that still looks healthy. I made staleness visible at three levels: the age on every response, a health check that fails once the board ages out, and a metric that a single alert can watch for both "never loaded" and "too old".

next: Connect it to the voice agent's load lookup, which is still a placeholder on the voice side, and pass the suggested question through to the LLM.
Distance search ("within 100 miles of Dallas") using zip-to-coordinate enrichment. The columns are already reserved.
Fuzzy city matching for speech-to-text variants such as "St. Louis" and "Saint Louis".
Persist each snapshot so any quote can be traced back to exactly what the agent saw.
lesson: Separate the decision from the phrasing. Code is good at applying consistent rules to data, and LLMs are good at turning a decision into natural speech. Letting each do only its own part made the dialog shorter, testable and predictable. I would also carry over the habit of treating staleness as part of the answer, not just an ops alert.
